toc.title: The relationship is the heart of therapy
What you should know a few sessions in
Reframe: "my system feels this way around this person"

blocks.p: A listener left a comment on my blog about two therapists: one she connected with, and one she isn't connecting with now. I want to use her story to get at the co-regulative relationship in therapy, and why it matters so much in getting unstuck, if you're in therapy. I don't know her. I'm only going on what she wrote, so I'm treating this as a general case.
She started with the first therapist:

q: I had this amazing therapist who I felt so safe with, and I was able to really process and grieve my trauma in such a transformative way that I felt like a new person after a year of seeing her. She was very engaging. She spoke in a prosodic way, always kept eye contact, and had a lot of reflecting to give me. She was emotive and, in turn, that really made me feel socially engaged with her, like she was really in it with me.

blocks.p: That's awesome. That's what we want, right? Someone who is warm, someone who is engaging, someone we feel connection with.

blocks.h: The relationship is the heart of therapy

blocks.p: Therapists can create this welcoming, comforting relationship, and that really is the ideal. That's at the heart of therapy.

Of course, not all therapists are the same. We're different in every possible way, including our personality, and specifically our capability of connection: our ability to socially engage and to create a warm, co-regulative environment. I'm not super social at all, but when it comes to therapy, I think I'm able to create that co-regulative environment well enough to help my clients.

A therapist who can provide the kind of warmth she's describing is probably going to establish rapport faster. Rapport, the therapeutic alliance, the relationship, is extremely important in outcomes for the client. If you don't have that safe, co-regulative relationship, I don't know how helpful therapy is going to be, or how helpful the specific techniques the therapist uses will be.
So if you're with someone you feel safe with, awesome. But if you don't really feel that rapport, that warmth, that connection, it's absolutely okay to change therapists, and it might be needed.

I don't think it has to have a super cozy feel. There were a few therapists I saw where I didn't have that. One of them was pretty combative with me. I didn't like him, but I benefited from him. There was enough trust there, enough something, that I really benefited. He put me on the spot and challenged me in a way I needed. I wasn't happy about it, but he was warm enough for me to accept his challenge, and he made an impact on me. We only met a couple of times.

So a warm, safe, co-regulative relationship is great. But it really comes down to this: do you feel like you can benefit from this person? Because it can go the opposite way, where they're giving you danger cues, and that can be a hindrance to the process of therapy. For the most part, trust your gut. You can intellectualize it and apply your understanding of the Polyvagal Theory too.
Here's where her story turns:

q: Fast-forward three years later, I decided to go back to therapy to just work on some personal and family things, this time with a whole new therapist because my old one wasn't available. I'm all excited to be in therapy again because of how transformative my first experience was, and my current therapy experience has been almost the opposite. I've been seeing my current one for about six months now, and to be honest, I feel like I've had no progress in really figuring out anything about my life, and I've oftentimes left appointments feeling like they accomplished nothing for me.

blocks.p: That's not a great initial sign, but it's not always a terrible sign either. Like I said, I clashed with that therapist at first, and he was actually very helpful.

Therapists are not always 100% on. This may come as a shock: I'm not a perfect therapist. I've made mistakes. At one point I had a session I completely bombed. It was not helpful, and I ended up giving my client a refund, because I did not bring my A game whatsoever.

blocks.h: What you should know a few sessions in

blocks.p: Still, I think a few sessions in, you should be able to tell whether this person is going to be helpful to you or not. By then:

ul: You should definitely know what kind of modality they're using.
You should have an idea of the rapport they're offering you, the feel of the relationship.
You should definitely have a treatment goal.

blocks.p: The feel may not be super warm and cozy. It might be more challenging. My clients usually tell me they want me to call them out on stuff, and that can totally happen, but with strong rapport. You can be warm and also challenging, caring and empathetic and also challenging.

Honestly, I usually feel like I'm able to build rapport after the first session. It's pretty rare that I can't make some kind of connection. At the end of most sessions I ask, "How'd this go for you? What could I do better? Did I do anything that was not helpful?" I ask my clients for feedback regularly.
So within a few sessions, I think you have a pretty good indication of whether someone is a good fit for you. That's my opinion, not a hard and fast rule.
She went on:

q: After reading the Polyvagal Theory, I learned about the nervous system states and our ability to read cues from our therapist that will put us in different states, which will affect what we're able to even process or feel. Something odd I noticed was that I always seemed to be so nervous before our sessions, and I never knew why. Like, I was super tense and anxious.

blocks.p: Yeah, absolutely. Feeling nervous before a session isn't necessarily abnormal, though. I think clients often feel a bit anxious before a session. We don't want to think about these things, we don't want to feel them. Clients often tell me, "I didn't want to show up to session. I did it anyway, and I'm really glad that I did." Therapy can be warm and cozy, but it can also be quite challenging. So I don't think it's necessarily a red flag to feel tense or anxious beforehand.

This comes down to being really honest with yourself. Not just her, all of us. The tension you might feel before therapy: is it because you're reluctant to work on yourself, or because the relationship with that therapist isn't a good fit? Both could be true.

No matter the modality, therapy should require some level of introspection, and that can be very anxiety-producing. It may require you to be brutally honest with yourself, about yourself or about past events in your life, depending on the therapist and how they work. With EMDR and trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy, talking about past events in detail is kind of standard. That could absolutely bring up some anxiety, maybe some aggression, maybe some collapse and disconnection too.
So ask yourself: what's the defensive state I feel before therapy?

ul: Is it my own stuff from that day?
Is it my own stuff, and worry about what may come up in therapy?
Is it about me and the modality of therapy?
Or is it between me and the therapist?

q: I was never nervous in therapy my first time around. My current therapist feels sort of like a blank slate. She often does not offer very much reflection back to me when I talk, and sometimes I feel the entire session I was the only one talking, and she may have said, like, four sentences total. She also does not speak very prosodically and oftentimes looks sort of glossy-eyed. Like, I can't tell if she's really engaged when I'm talking. This would make my anxiety go way up in session, and I felt like I was grasping at straws waiting for her to give me something helpful.

blocks.p: Ooh. That blank slate stuff, I don't think it works for everybody. It's not a style I'd be interested in as a client. I like the co-regulative aspect of working with a therapist, or a coach. I work with a coach too, and that co-regulation is something I needed.

The blank slate is what she describes: the therapist is quiet, with no facial affect, a very neutral presentation. That's how I remember being taught in therapy school. I don't know whether that's how it's taught now.

I think the purpose of the blank slate is to raise anxiety and provoke introspection: the client fills in the silence, maybe has some honest catharsis, some letting go of stuff, some relief. And I think there can be some utility there. Allowing some silence for the client to sit with whatever they're going through is definitely useful. But it's not for everybody, and maybe especially not at the start, during rapport building, before the client has felt you out. Before we can allow more of that silence, it may be important to have more back and forth, more warmth, more co-regulation.

The blank slate does not provide cues of safety. There's no facial affect. There's no vocal prosody. There's no eyebrow movement to show emotion, no upper cheek movement, no eye crinkles, no squints, no smiles. It's really the opposite of co-regulation. Co-regulation is those unconscious cues of safety we send to our clients that are so helpful.

So that biobehavioral connection is missing. Even if the therapist's safety state is there, it's not being shown or shared. The therapist isn't giving cues of safety to help the client calm their nervous system, and that's what co-regulation is.

That means the intended catharsis may not happen. It may leave the client exposed to their traumatic memories or feelings, or just to the anxiety that surfaces, with no relief. It lingers. There's no discharge. There's no ladder climbing. There's no access to the safety state. They're accessing the defensive state, maybe even consciously, maybe they feel it, but they lack the capacity to feel it mindfully, to describe it and share it, because you have to have the safety state active in order to feel the more defensive stuff.
So instead of helping, I think for a lot of clients the blank slate is going to be detrimental, and might even reinforce the stuck defensive state.

If a client can access their safety state and self-regulate, the blank slate may be more helpful. They can fill in the space. They can use their own introspection and their capacity for stillness, to be safe and immobile, to look inward and share. The therapist becomes someone they bounce ideas off, building insight together. But for the majority of clients, especially the ones with more dysregulation, which is kind of why you go to therapy, the blank slate might reinforce the stuck state.
I don't think the point of therapy is to induce anxious catharsis. I think the point of therapy is to help clients build self-regulation, and that's done through co-regulation.

Self-regulation is not something we're born with. Many of our clients, many of mine, did not get healthy attachment or co-regulation when they were younger, so their capacity to self-regulate is lower. They need to experience co-regulation, a healthy relationship, healthy boundaries. Therapy can provide all of those things, and that's the foundation for the client to eventually build self-regulation. Once they have enough of it, maybe letting them sit in silence with their feelings can be of help.

I'm fairly active as a therapist, but I definitely allow some silence when it's needed. With a couple of clients, I've flat out said, "Hey, we're going to sit in silence. I want you to just feel what's going on inside of you, and I'm going to give you ten seconds of silence." I give it a finite amount of time. Then I may stretch it to fifteen or twenty seconds, not much longer. Instead of talking, talking, talking, I want them to actually feel what's happening inside instead of trying to explain it. And that's only if I think they can handle it.

q: I wanted to feel connected to her. It was hard to explain this feeling because I kept telling myself that she was a good therapist because sometimes she'd say all the right things, but I didn't feel like she was engaged with me? It was hard to grasp why I felt so weird in our sessions. After reading the Polyvagal Theory, I feel like it's because of the nervous system state she provoked me to enter. I would often feel embarrassed telling traumatizing stories or like I was being a burden. It's taken me a whole lot of sessions to realize that I don't think she guides me to a safe state, and that's why I feel like I've made no progress in our sessions, even after SIX MONTHS of seeing her. Sometimes our sessions feel like I'm just filling her in on my life, and it's like talking to a wall. I keep waiting to feel something, but it never happens.

blocks.p: I'm sorry to hear that. First, let me absolutely validate this whole sentiment. I can see why somebody would feel uncomfortable, and then start to assume things like being a burden.

We know story follows state. When we feel uncomfortable, when we're in more defensive states, our mind comes up with reasons why. It creates an explanation, and that explanation probably has a lot to do with the larger themes in our life, and more often than not, with the themes we were taught growing up.

blocks.h: Reframe: "my system feels this way around this person"

blocks.p: Now I want to empower all of us with a reframe. Instead of saying, "My therapist causes me this feeling," I invite you to say, "My system feels this way when I'm around this person."

When we blame other people for our feelings, it gives them a lot of power over us. Of course, some people are deserving of blame. That's fine. And of course we have feelings based on what's happening around us. I get it. But in cases like this, the reframe invites more of a mindful witnessing of what's happening, rather than being the victim of how someone's making you feel.

So instead of "My therapist is causing me to feel this," you can say, "My body shifts to an anxious flight state when I'm around my therapist." Or, "My body shifts to a defensive state, and then my mind comes up with an explanation: I'm a burden, no one likes me, I'm not worth working on," whatever stories we come up with. There's no blame in that. It's a statement of fact. You're noticing how you feel, as a witness to your nervous system state.

If you're in the position of "this person is causing this," there's not a whole lot of hope there. But when you can objectively say, "I feel this way around this person," there's more space to ask, "My system feels this way. What do I want to do about that? What options do I have?"

It's a small reframe, and it's not just about therapists. Rather than "My parents make me feel this way," you could say, "I notice that when I'm around my parents, I get really anxious. I go into more of a flight state." "My parents make me feel pissed off" feels like it's up for debate, or like you're blaming, and then they blame you back, and it goes on forever. But "I feel more aggressive when I'm around this family member" opens up some capacity for noticing, and maybe curiosity. Then you can ask yourself, "How much time do I want to spend around this person? How much time do I want my nervous system to be in their presence?" I think there's more capacity to make an objective decision there than when you're stuck in a blame cycle.

That may be especially true in a professional relationship. "I get really anxious when this plumber comes into my house" is a lot different from "This plumber makes me feel anxious." It's very similar, but instead of being a victim, you're noticing it. And the next time you hire a plumber, why would you hire the person you feel flight energy around? Same thing for therapists.
She wrapped up:

q: In conclusion, I'm probably going to stop seeing her soon. But I myself know that truly powerful therapy is totally possible with the right person. I just thought I'd share my story about therapy and how even a totally regular and seemingly normal therapist can completely change a client's effectiveness in session.

blocks.p: Thank you for sharing it. I spend time on the podcast talking about bad therapy, things that are egregiously bad. But the reality is that most of what's not helpful in therapy is just status quo therapy. It's what we were trained in: a focus on techniques, anxiety about getting techniques right, modalities, following manuals, instead of building rapport with the client, and self-regulation first, with co-regulation coming from that.

I think that's probably a big issue, and it's something I monitor in myself constantly as a therapist: how self-regulated am I? The less self-regulated I am, the less effective I am. When I'm really self-regulated and in my safety state, I'm a much more effective therapist. So what's not helpful in therapy probably isn't the big unethical, unlawful, non-therapeutic things. It's the stuff we get swept up in through our own anxieties, like doing the blank slate when it's not appropriate, or because it helps us feel better in a session.

So reflect on the people in your life, including us therapists, and ask: how does my nervous system feel around this person? Then the follow-up: how much time do I want to give them? And for a professional relationship like a therapist: do I want to give them any more time at all, or do I want to see how I feel around somebody else who might provide the same service, possibly even more effectively?
